# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-26 (Extended v183)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 7. Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Marché Saint-Jean, Rue des Billettes, Rue Saint-Denis, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, Rue Mondétour, Pointe Saint-Eustache, Rue du Cygne, Rue des Prêcheurs, Rue Blomet, Rue de Rivoli, Place Louis XV, Champs-Élysées, Esplanade, bridge of the Invalides, Hôtel des Princes, Hôtel Meurice, Rue Saint-Honoré, Passage Delorme, Place du Palais-Royal, Rue de Béthisy, Rue des Bourdonnais, Rue de la Poterie, Rue du Contrat-Social, Marché-aux-Poirées, Rue de Babylone, Rue du Chaume, Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes, Royal Printing Establishment, Luxembourg Garden. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Wilholt, Torton, Quenford, Pontoise, Stenenridge, Gulhaven. Barrière d'Enfer, Esplanade de l'Observatoire.

**Rumored claims (unverified)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately (winter Year 5). Fenelle Lindmere and Marald confided/revealed Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. Ferald Stenworth confided to Zavus Prydenridge that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood (autumn Year 6). **Claim (from new text): In letter Ismira Stenson burned after reading, Elra revealed deed to Kelmere pastures was forged**.

**Established facts**: Kassa Brackick and Volan Stenworth married at Staveford; Kassa later went to Dungate. Taric Corrley quit Staveford, took lodgings in Dungate. Marald Corrford quit Dunstead, took lodgings in Salcombe; Fenelle Lindmere followed within month. Ismira Stenson quit Dungate, took lodgings in Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Matho Stenson went to Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Elra Corrford settled in Elmhaven. Havie Prydenridge promised Gadrek Prydenridge to pay old debt to Stenworth family. Kassa Stenson's husband gave solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Fenelle Lindmere found work in Elmhaven, moved there, did not return to Salcombe (summer Year 7). Marald Corrford followed to Elmhaven within the month (summer Year 7). **Zavus Prydenridge apprenticed anew and became ferryman (new change, summer Year 7)**.

**Solemn promises (established)**: Elra Corrford gave Matho Stenson solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven. Pelia gave Fenelle solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe (summer Year 7).

**New births and marriages (Spring Year 7)**: Rinelle Corrley and Kadrek Brackick had son Movus Brackick (Wilholt). Nerine Prydenridge and Lurald Stenworth wed at Ostcombe, lived thereafter, had son Istho Stenworth (Ostcombe). Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge had son Febin Prydenridge (Kelmere). Bremira Corrford and Zavus Prydenridge married at Dunstead, lived thereafter.

**Spring and Summer Year 7 observations**: Residents walked long way to avoid muddy square. Road rutted and puddled after thaw. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall (repeated observations). Multiple residents hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Yera, Rinelle, Zavus, Kadan, Bremira, Rorald Lindmere). Matho, Bremira, Thizek, and Pelia each counted coins twice, came up penny short. Taric remarked river was up at Dungate crossing; Kassa said it always was in spring. Sebin remarked river was up; Rorald Lindmere said it always was in spring. **Elra remarked river was up; Fenelle Lindmere said it always was in spring**. **Ismira asked if it would rain; Fenelle only shrugged**. Ismira and Bremira each argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Ferald Stenworth argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Kadan and Rovus talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rovus and Kadan discussed scandal of salt prices. Bremira and Ferald discussed scandal of salt prices. Yewyn and Pelia discussed scandal of salt prices. Yera laughed at story nobody else found funny. Sebin and Rorald Lindmere laughed at stories nobody else found funny. Pelia Lindmere laughed at story nobody else found funny. **Bremira Corrford laughed at story nobody else found funny**. **Thizek Stenenridge laughed at story nobody else found funny**. Yera Stenworth and Zavus complained of aching backs. Pelia complained of aching back, as usual. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Yewyn Haskick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. Tatho Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. **Isvie Stenworth bought ribbon at stall and regretted it**. Yewyn appeared tired; Pelia noted this. Tatho mended torn sleeve by window and said little. **Bremira mended torn sleeve by window and said little**. **Zavus Prydenridge mended torn sleeve by window and said little**. **Fenelle Lindmere mended torn sleeve by window and said little (Elmhaven)**. "Will it rain, do you think?" asked Tatho. Rorald only shrugged. Tatho spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Baker's boy was late again, line at oven grew long. "You look tired," Thizek Stenenridge told Zavus Prydenridge, who did not deny it. Rorald Lindmere walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Zavus read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints. Isvie Stenworth fell asleep in chair before fire had caught. **Bremira fell asleep in chair before fire had caught**. Rain threatened since morning but held off.

**Summer Year 7 broken faith**: Rorald Lindmere broke faith with Kassa Stenson—promised work (carry sealed letter to Torton) never begun.

## Jean Valjean's Crisis and Discovery
**Blotting-book discovery (night 24th June 1832)**: Upon arriving at Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings, Valjean found Cosette's blotting-book open on sideboard. Mirror reflection revealed four lines—letter Cosette wrote to young workman in Rue Plumet. Valjean understood Cosette was escaping; another was goal of her heart. Soul gave utter roar. Into paternity his life's widowhood introduced all shades of love—daughter, mother, sister, woman, wife. Grief surpassed bounds; quiver of revolt ran head to foot; immense reawakening of egotism; the *I* howled.

**During Spring Year 7**: Groped up stairs, hand trembling greatly. Unfolded Marius's note announcing death and love. Seized essential points. Beheld splendor of death of hated individual, remained crushed with intoxicated amazement. **Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings**: Two sleeping-rooms, dining-room, kitchen, garret for Toussaint on second floor, back court. Initially slept well; awoke almost gay; recovered serenity and security. Twice or thrice Toussaint stammered about fighting in Paris—Valjean paid no heed, absorbed in calculations.

**Current state (summer Year 7)**: Valjean asleep; Toussaint has not risen. Cosette's father thought unkind by her. **Valjean at barricade (6th June, dawn)**: Took aim at fireman acting as sentinel on neighboring roof, smashed his helmet with bullet. When officer replaced sentinel, Valjean took aim again, sent officer's casque to join soldier's. Officer retired speedily. No further attempts to spy on barricade made thereafter.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance
**Recognition and love**: Cosette acknowledged she never forgot Marius, always loved him. Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening, forcing old gate. At height of love's voluptuousness, remained absolutely chaste. **Confessions (spring Year 6, during cholera)**: Marius told Cosette—orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, father colonel and hero on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. Cosette told Marius—brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father M. Fauchelevent. **Éponine's death (evening 24th June)**: Éponine revealed she led Marius to barricade, spoke of her death as blessing, protected him from gunfire. Gave Marius letter from Cosette before dying. **Cosette's letter content**: Marriage impossible; grandfather refuses; no fortune either; hastened to him, he gone; kept promise given; dies; loves him. **Marius's response**: Covered letter with kisses; reflected Cosette going to England. Resolved to inform Cosette of death, send farewell, save Gavroche.

**Marius joins barricade (evening 24th June)**: Upon learning Valjean plans England departure in one week, arranged meeting 26th June at nine o'clock. Same evening, displaced bar at grating, rushed in. Cosette absent. Seated self with resolution, blessed love. Mad with grief, one desire: speedy end. Voice summoned him to barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie. **During first phase**: Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed; flung self into conflict. Saved Gavroche with first shot, delivered Courfeyrac with second. Seized powder barrel, dropped flame with startling cry. **Mental state (6th June, dawn)**: Fasting, fevered, emerged from all hope, stranded in grief, saturated with violent emotions, conscious end was near, plunged into visionary stupor voluntarily accepted. Despair's ecstasy. Felt he had entered tomb.

**Cosette's current state (summer Year 7, morning)**: Slept only few hours but soundly; had sweet dreams. Awoke with sun in eyes. First thought smiling. Felt thoroughly reassured. Began cherishing hope without knowing why. Then felt pang at heart. Three days since saw Marius. Certain he would come today, perhaps this very morning. Felt she could not live without Marius. Opened window, looked around hoping to see street. Back court surrounded by high walls, outlook only on gardens. Pronounced gardens hideous; for first time found flowers ugly. Decided to gaze at sky, thought Marius might come from that quarter. Burst into tears. Heard sharp shocks in distance—actually cannon reports battering barricade. **Cosette at window (6th June, dawn)**: Observed martin's nest in ancient cornice below her window. Mother spread wings like fan over brood; father fluttered about, bearing food and kisses. Gilded by dawning day. Great law "Multiply" lay there smiling and august. Sweet mystery unfolded in morning's glory. Cosette, hair in sunlight, soul absorbed in chimæras, illuminated by love within and dawn without, bent over mechanically and began gazing at birds, family, male and female, mother and little ones, with profound trouble virgin nest produces.

## Barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie (24th June into 6th June)
**Café Corinthe**: Ground floor with bar; first floor with billiard-table and spiral staircase; cellar via trap-door; lodgings and attics. Proprietor: Widow Hucheloup. Serving-maids: Matelote, Gibelotte. **Two barricades**: Larger shut off Rue de la Chanvrerie; other closed Rue Mondétour. **Larger barricade (6th June, dawn)**: Height six or seven feet, stepped construction, paling-stones, casks, wheels, omnibus pole with ropes, red flag. Forty-three insurgents. **Three-front fortification**: Walled on Rue de la Chanvrerie (front), Rues du Cygne and de la Petite Truanderie (left), Rue Mondétour (right). Almost impregnable but fatally hemmed in. No exit.

**Javert's arrest**: Identified as Inspector of Police, aged fifty-two. Bound with whip-cord about feet, martingale rope from neck. Upon seeing Valjean surveying him, remarked: "It is perfectly simple."

**Le Cabuc execution**: Enjolras executed him for killing, justified by insurrection needing discipline.

**M. Mabeuf's sacrifice**: Venerable, austere, aged eighty. Evening 24th June: followed band, refused arms. During attack: tore flag from Enjolras, upholding red banner with aged arm. Enjolras eulogized: magnificent death; presence renders barricade impregnable. Body lay in kitchen on table.

**Gavroche's role (6th June)**: Young gamin, fearless, collected cartridges under heavy fire. Scampered, teased fusillade, retorted to discharges with couplets. National Guardsmen and soldiers laughed while aiming at him. Called invulnerable dwarf of the fray, stranger gamin-fairy, played hide and seek with death. One better-aimed bullet finally struck him; Gavroche staggered and sank. Whole barricade cried out. He remained in sitting posture, long thread of blood streaked face, raised both arms, glanced toward shot's direction, began to sing. **Gavroche's origins and current state**: Same children over whom Gavroche had been put to trouble earlier (reader's recollection). Children of Thénardiers, leased to Magnon, attributed to M. Gillenormand, now lost leaves swept by wind. Their clothing converted to rags. **Two lost children (same as Gavroche had known) in Luxembourg Garden (6th June, daytime)**: One aged seven, one aged five, pale and ragged like wild birds. Smaller said "I am very hungry." Escaped from guardhouse, mountebank's booth, or passed night in sentry-box after evading inspectors at closing hour. Stray lambs, seemed free but were lost. Slipped into garden contrary to regulations; closed gates and slack oversight allowed them to remain.

**Tactical situation (6th June)**: Unknown messenger announced whole army of Paris striking, third bearing down, National Guard advancing, attack in one hour. After first assault and repairs: insurgents rallied, majority ascended to first-story window. Medical students cared for wounded. Five gravely wounded men on mattresses in kitchen converted to ambulance. Barricade repaired and augmented, raised two feet. No repast possible; fifty men exhausted scanty provisions during sixteen hours. Enjolras placed veto on fifteen hermetically sealed bottles found in cellar. Insurgents full of hope, smiled waiting for dawn attack, reckoned succor on way, divided day into three phases: six o'clock—regiment would turn; noon—insurrection of all Paris; sunset—revolution.

**Cannon and musketry**: Musketry and grape-shot alternated without great ravages. Top of Corinthe façade suffered; windows riddled, slowly losing shape. Mattress placed on roof of six-story house fell outside barricade. Eight-pounder brass cannon crew attacked; whole barricade fired but missed. Flame leaped from insurgent rifle, artillery-man turned twice with arms extended, head uplifted, fell with side on gun, ball traversed breast side to side. Dead. After sergeant's death, exasperated troop opened fire. Two cannons attacked redoubt from Rue de la Chanvrerie; two others from Rue Saint-Denis and Rue Aubry-le-Boucher riddled Saint-Merry barricade. Four cannons echoed mournfully. Combatants driven from crest by balls, from windows by grape-shot. Columns ventured into street, attempted to scale redoubt. Barricade long silent, then poured forth desperate fire; seven or eight discharges followed with rage and joy. Street filled with blinding smoke. Two thirds of gunners distinguished lying beneath wheels of cannons. Fire slackened. Smoke filled street, created twilight in daylight. Combatants could hardly see each other.

**Broader insurrection (6th June morning)**: Barricades begun in Rue du Poirier and Rue des Gravilliers. Young man armed with rifle attacked cavalry squadron, killed commander, remarked "There's another who will do us no more harm," was put to sword. Woman fired on National Guard from behind lowered blind in Rue Saint-Denis. Child aged fourteen arrested with pockets full of cartridges. Entrance to Rue Bertin-Poirée received lively fusillade. Marshal Soult grew thoughtful, recalled saying at Saragossa about old women emptying chamber pots on soldiers' heads. Military chiefs made haste to stamp out conflagration sparks, delayed attack on barricades until larger disturbances suppressed.

**Enjolras on insurrection and repression**: Insurrection speedily exhausted, has only certain number of shots and combatants. Empty cartridge-box and dead man cannot be replaced. Repression has army, does not count men; has Vincennes, does not count shots. Struggles of one against hundred always crush barricade unless revolution flings flaming archangel's sword into balance. Then everything rises, pavements seethe, popular redoubts abound, Paris quivers supremely, *quid divinum* given forth, a 10th of August or 29th of July in air, wonderful light appears, yawning maw of force draws back, army sees before it erect and tranquil that prophet, France.

**Bossuet on Enjolras**: Admires Enjolras's impassive temerity. Lives alone, renders him sad; complains his greatness binds him to widowhood. Rest have mistresses who make them crazy, that is, brave. Woman sets man off. Enjolras has no woman, not in love, yet intrepid—thing unheard of.

**Combeferre's philosophy**: Quoted and discussed classical figures—Harmodius and Aristogiton, Brutus, Chereas, Stephanus, Cromwell, Charlotte Corday, Sand. Discussion on Brutus and Cæsar: Cæsar fell justly; his twenty-three wounds touch less than spitting in face of Jesus Christ. Christ cuffed by lackeys. One feels God through greater outrage. When no more kings, no more war. Remarked sergeant was charming young man, intrepid, thoughtful, well-educated, probably in love, not more than five and twenty.
